categories.justification: Addresses the approve/reject decision directly. Covers all three mustFlag issues (fast hash unsuitable, per-minute/per-second error, digest length irrelevant) plus the areas an expert would expect: compliance, migration risk, DoS/rate limiting, cost-preserving alternatives. Nothing in it is padding.
quotes: The memo's 1,000-core figure comes from a 60x unit error
Password-storage strength comes from cost per guess (work factor or memory hardness), not digest length.

categories.justification: Every numeric claim checks out: 16.7 cores, 60x, 19.68 vCPU, 625,000x, 184/2^7 extrapolation. Search-snippet sources (NIST, PCI, AWS pricing) are classed as INFERRED, and estimates are labelled as extrapolations rather than overstated. I found no material errors.
quotes: 4,000 per minute is about 66.7 per second. At 0.25 CPU-s each that is about 16.7 cores
This is an estimate, not a measured cost-12 benchmark.
The NIST and PCI text come from search snippets only and were not fetched in full

categories.justification: Explains the mechanisms: why a salt does not slow guessing, and why digest length is not what limits an attacker. Quantifies attacker speed-up, cost, burst load and Argon2id memory. Covers edge cases such as a breach mid-migration and rate-limit bypass.
quotes: A per-user salt only stops guesses from being shared across users or precomputed. It does not make each guess slower.
Breach during the memo's migration: the database would hold bcrypt hashes for inactive users and fast SHA-256 hashes for active users
an unmitigated burst implies about 5.6 GiB of concurrent hashing memory

categories.justification: Challenges both premises in the memo and the finance framing. Takes the strongest counterarguments seriously, including DoS concerns and the GPU extrapolation. States what further evidence would change the conclusion.
quotes: The hashcat bcrypt figure is only an extrapolation, so the GPU speed-up may be overstated. — That is true
uses OWASP's rehash-on-login mechanism in reverse
FIPS alignment would change the recommended fallback from Argon2id to PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256.

categories.justification: Gives a clear verdict with concrete, conditional next steps: return the memo with corrected numbers, choose between secure alternatives, measure hashing CPU and rate-limit pass-through, and confirm compliance scope.
quotes: Do not approve the SHA-256 switch. Return the memo with the corrected core arithmetic
Instrument hashing CPU separately from other auth-service CPU
Measure how many burst attempts reach the hashing tier before right-sizing the 48 vCPU cluster.

categories.justification: Well organised. Claims are tied to evidence IDs and to calculations that were re-run, and uncertainty is explicitly labelled throughout.
quotes: These are order-of-magnitude proxies, not the company's actual spend.

mustFlagAdjudication.quote: OWASP explicitly calls fast hashes such as SHA-256 unsuitable for password storage.
4,000 logins per minute at 0.25 CPU-s needs about 16.7 cores, not 1,000.
Output digest length (256 vs 184 bits) does not determine password-hashing strength.

criticalFailures.condition: Recommends or accepts migrating password storage to single-iteration salted SHA-256
criticalFailures.evidence: "Reject the proposal as written." / "Do not choose any fast hash."

criticalFailures.condition: Accepts the 1,000-core figure without correcting it
criticalFailures.evidence: "The memo's core count is wrong by a factor of 60... about 16.7 cores at peak"

notesForHumanAdjudicator: Very strong output that matches the reference summary on every point. One small imprecision: it implies bcrypt has no memory hardness ("which bcrypt and SHA-256 lack"), when bcrypt uses a small fixed amount of memory. This is common phrasing and not material. I did not open the supplied fixture documents. The numbers it cites as coming from them match the request and the reference.
